transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Time: 4:00 PM PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Ng (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Halo Head of ML), Tom Ellis (Eng Manager), Aisha Khan (Security), Ben Carter (Frontend)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood, and with me is Marcus our solutions engineer. Quick check, is this time still good?
[00:06] Priya Sharma: Yep all good, thanks. We were excited to see the SDK flow.
[00:10] Marcus Ng: Awesome, we'll focus on the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, auth patterns, env setup and then run a short demo of the API and Console. If questions come up, interrupt.
[00:18] Tom Ellis: Great. Side note, budget and latency are the two things we are watching closely.
[00:22] Lena Park: Totally understood. We'll point out tradeoffs and what to change for lower latency vs lower cost.
[00:27] Marcus Ng: Alright starting with the Python quickstart. The repo is a tiny pip package, main entry is examples/generate.py. You pip install redwood-inference (note: package name may change, repo link coming). The pattern is: set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an environment variable, then instantiate the client and call client.generate or client.chat depending on your flow. Example: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(); out = client.generate(model='gpt-3b-redwood', prompt='Summarize...')
[00:54] Ben Carter: Is that package synchronous only or async? Our frontend infra uses serverless with async handlers.
[00:59] Marcus Ng: Good call — the SDK has both sync and async. In Python we expose async client via redwood.aio.RedwoodAsyncClient. The quickstart shows both. For serverless we recommend the async client and short timeouts.
[01:12] Priya Sharma: Ok and for TypeScript?
[01:14] Marcus Ng: For TS it's similar: import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.generate({ model: '...'}); We also have streaming support with EventSource/streams in the browser and node.
[01:31] Tom Ellis: For browser usage — any concerns with exposing keys?
[01:34] Lena Park: We recommend proxying through your backend. You can also use short-lived tokens and our token exchange flow if you want frontend direct streaming. We'll send the quickstart patterns.
[01:43] Aisha Khan: Security question: does Redwood support SSO/SAML for service accounts or just API keys?
[01:48] Marcus Ng: Right now the main auth for API calls is API keys; for enterprise and Private deployments we support SSO for the console and IAM integration with service accounts. For key rotation and secrets management you can integrate with your KMS — the hosted control plane supports KMS-backed keys for higher security.
[02:05] Aisha Khan: Do you have docs on KMS integration and audit logs? We need SOC 2 columns and detailed audit trails.
[02:12] Lena Park: Yes, we'll share the security pack. We have SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001 artifacts, and logs — and for Private you can forward audit events to your SIEM. Marcus, maybe touch on audit logs?
[02:22] Marcus Ng: Sure. On Hosted we keep request-level logs for X days (configurable add-on). Audit logs for admin actions are available via the console, and you can stream them to your logging buckets. On Dedicated/Private, you control log retention and can integrate with your KMS/HSM for encryption.
[02:38] Priya Sharma: Good. For the POC we'll probably start with hosted but need encryption-at-rest and tenant isolation assurances.
[02:46] Lena Park: That's a common path. Start hosted for speed, then move to Dedicated if you need stronger isolation or throughput guarantees. We can size a dedicated pool later.
[02:54] Marcus Ng: Back to SDK — environment variables: we suggest REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_REGION (for routing), and REDWOOD_MODEL_OVERRIDE if you want to pin models. The quickstart includes an .env.example. For local dev you can set them, for CI we recommend secret manager integrations.
[03:14] Ben Carter: Any config for batching? Our customers send short chat messages and we want efficient token cost.
[03:19] Marcus Ng: Yes, batching is on the server; you can control max_batch_size and latency SLO via route config. In the SDK you can set request.metadata with hints like prefer_low_latency: true; those flow into smart routing. We'll share sample route config.
[03:34] Priya Sharma: Can you show the demo call?
[03:36] Marcus Ng: Yep — switching to terminal. (typing) Example: python examples/generate.py --prompt "Summarize last week's orders". You'll see a streaming response, tokens arrive in chunks.
[03:48] [03:48] Marcus Ng: (demo) streaming response — here's a small note, if you are using Node, use the stream handler to pipe partial tokens to the client.
[04:02] Tom Ellis: Latency numbers?
[04:04] Marcus Ng: For the model we demoed, median p95 is around 180ms per token on our dedicated configs for this sequence length. On hosted it depends on load; we'll share profiler numbers. For short sequences you can expect sub-1s for a 20 token response in many regions.
[04:23] Priya Sharma: Sounds reasonable. For benchmarking, can you provide sample payloads?
[04:27] Marcus Ng: Yes, sample payloads and a benchmark harness. I'll attach the harness in the follow-up.
[04:33] Aisha Khan: Regarding data residency — we need EU data to stay in EU region.
[04:37] Lena Park: We support region pinning and can ensure data doesn't leave selected geo. For Private you can fully control network boundaries.
[04:44] Ben Carter: Any gotchas with TypeScript SDK and bundlers?
[04:46] Marcus Ng: We maintain both ESM and CJS builds. For browser you'd import the runtime-lite package. Watch for stream polyfills in older browsers — our quickstart mentions node-fetch or web streams polyfill.
[04:59] Tom Ellis: POC success criteria: 1) latency p95 < 800ms for our chat flow, 2) cost under $X per 1000 calls (TBD), 3) SOC2 checklist satisfied.
[05:10] Priya Sharma: Agreed. Also need a short A/B of model variants for quality.
[05:14] Lena Park: We'll help with model selection and quantization profiles via Redwood Optimize — Marcus will include a small suggestion doc.
[05:21] Marcus Ng: Quick note on fallbacks: if a high-accuracy model isn't available we can route to a slightly cheaper variant. The SDK supports model hints and automatic fallbacks in the route policy.
[05:33] [05:33] Marcus Ng: Ok jump to an example TypeScript file — (screen) index.ts: const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const res = await client.chat.create({ messages: [{ role: 'user', content: '...' }], model: 'redwood-chat-4k' }); console.log(res.choices[0].message.content);
[05:52] Ben Carter: Does the SDK return delta tokens for streaming or full final message only?
[05:56] Marcus Ng: Both. Streaming returns deltas, final call returns full message. We also provide guidance on how to reconcile partial and final messages in flaky networks.
[06:08] Priya Sharma: Aisha any security follow-ups?
[06:10] Aisha Khan: I'd like to see the KMS architecture diagram and proof of key rotation, and details on how audit logs include per-token request id mapping back to user ids.
[06:20] Lena Park: We'll include those in the security pack. Also worth noting for Private you can keep keys in your HSM and we never see raw model inputs if you want end-to-end control.
[06:31] Tom Ellis: Onboarding effort — how long to get POC up?
[06:34] Lena Park: If you start hosted and use the quickstart, teams get a simple flow in under a day to make calls. To integrate with infra and SSO and do benchmark testing expect 1-2 weeks.
[06:45] Priya Sharma: Good. Any pricing edge cases for high-throughput?
[06:48] Marcus Ng: For high throughput we recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity for predictable pricing. We can model cost vs latency with your sample traffic.
[06:56] Ben Carter: If we want to stream from browser for live typing indicators, do you have rate limits?
[07:00] Marcus Ng: Yes we have rate limits; for real-time streaming we have burst rules and recommend using dedicated pools or edge routing. We'll share recommended rate limit settings for live typing.
[07:12] Priya Sharma: Can you confirm SDK versioning strategy? We want stable APIs.
[07:16] Lena Park: Semver for SDKs, breaking changes announced ahead of time, and we support pinning to client minor versions in your package.json and runtime. Also our Console lets you pin model versions.
[07:28] Marcus Ng: Wrapping up demo — I'll drop the quickstart links and the small sample harness.
[07:34] [07:34] Lena Park: Recap: we'll send Python and TypeScript quickstarts, security pack (SOC2/ISO/KMS details), benchmark harness and sample payloads, and propose POC kickoff time.
[07:46] Priya Sharma: That sounds great. Can we aim to have the POC kickoff week of 12/14?
[07:50] Lena Park: Yes we can do that. Marcus, are you available that week for the deep technical session?
[07:55] Marcus Ng: Yep. I'll block time for the POC kickoff and a deeper performance run.
[07:59] Aisha Khan: Also send the DPA and any compliance docs for legal.
[08:04] Lena Park: Will do.
[08:07] Tom Ellis: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[08:09] Ben Carter: Thanks.
[08:10] Priya Sharma: Thanks, bye.
[08:12] Lena Park: Bye all, we'll follow up with links.

[41:30] End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: some product names transcribed oddly (Redwood often shows as Redwood Inferance or RedwoodInfr). There are a few timestamp jumps and filler words.
